messages.author: 58ada370762d4351
messages.subject: Speeding up fitting models
parts:
Hi all

I'm hoping for some general advice on speeding up fitting some models in secr. I have 90 traps (cameras, sight-only) over about 45 daily occasions. The study area is a small island that has a full trapping grid so I'm using a polygon of the island as a mask. It takes several minutes on 30 cores just to fit a null model (D ~ 1) with an approx 140m grid (default from make.mask) and much much longer when introducing some covariates.

What would be some areas I could add efficiency without compromising the predictions? E.g. would it make much of a difference to reduce the detection data to counts per trap rather than using daily occasions? Is there benefit in increasing the spacing in make.mask? Or is this just to be expected with these types of models?

As an aside, I often get warnings that there are "invalid distribution for sighting at Eval [number]" - where would this be coming from? 

Thanks

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Speeding up fitting models
parts:
Hi Simeon

Yes, that sounds really slow.

The first question is Do you really have sighting only data? This might be needed if some unknown fraction of animals are visually identifiable while the rest aren't. If they are all identifiable then don't use mark-resight. I haven't looked at mark-resight for a long time... checking the C++ code I see that the sighting-only calculations make _no_ use of multithreading (timing hasn't been an issue), so your extra cores are wasted.

How many points are there in your habitat mask? You can usually increase the mask spacing without affecting estimates up to about sigma/2 (see e.g. https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-habitatmasks.pdf). Collapsing occasions is routine with binary proximity data, and doesn't affect estimates. I'm not 100% sure with sighting data, but it is probably OK and you could simulate some data and check.

The warning indicates an inconsistency between the data and the model that can be ignored if it is transient and secr.fit produces estimates with SE.

Murray

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Speeding up fitting models
parts:
I'm wary of giving advice because I am rusty on this, but...

Mark-resight and capture-recapture relate to different data types. In capture-recapture every individual detected for the first time becomes individually distinguishable (marked) from then on. This works if all individuals carry natural marks. In mark-resight, the only distinguishable individuals are those in the 'marked' fraction of the population, either because of a preceding marking phase, or because they have permanent natural marks; sightings of other (unmarked) individuals are counted and contribute to the population estimate on the assumption that they share detection parameters with the marked animals.

In your sighting-only scenario with natural marks, all marking effectively happened (naturally) before the start of the study. We assume unmarked animals are distributed spatially just like the marked animals (marking is random with respect to location).

I'm still puzzled that fitting takes so long. If you are able to send me an example offline (data, mask, code) I'll try to track down the problem (may take a few days).

Murray

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Speeding up fitting models
parts:
Hi

I was able to tease out some of the issues with the (very tidy) data sent offline.

Mark-resight is tricky, frustrating, and prone to difficulties with model fitting, as you found.

Your use case is common enough and should be covered better in the documentation. An unknown fraction of the population carry natural marks.

The reason your model fits so quickly when you treat these as capture-recapture data (markocc all 1) rather than sighting-only mark-resight (markocc all zero) is that 'secr.fit' by default then collapses all occasions. This 'fastproximity' option is never invoked for sighting data, but you can emulate it manually as we will see.

Your initial data were of detector type 'count' (strictly 'count proximity' - potentially more than one detection per individual per camera per occasion). Binary proximity data (detector type 'proximity') are much faster to model. I also prefer proximity data in this case because they reduce potential pseudo-replication from repeat photographs at the same camera.

As I understand it, the data do not include a sighting category 'seen to be marked but not identified' (Tm NULL). Then we fix the parameter pID to avoid estimating it. Also for unknown marks we set the details argument knownmarks = FALSE.

Collapsing occasions is fairly simple - just use the reduce method for capthist objects with by = 'all' and a suitable outputdetector.
A coarser mask is justifiable - especially for exploration. For this dataset the spatial extent is set by the coastline and details distribution = 'binomial' is probably appropriate.

Here is a demonstration. Do not believe model fits with very small SE (e.g. fits[[3]] and perhaps sigma-hat from fits[[1]]). Remember these data are quirky, with many repeats at the same camera and a few camera-addicted individuals.

Murray

# mask250 is a 250-m mask
# cats_capts_sight is the full initial capthist dataset (46 occasions, includes sightings of unmarked Tu).

change detector type to 'proximity'
# dropunused set FALSE to avoid dropping occasion with zero detections
cats_capts_sight_proximity <- reduce( cats_capts_sight, output = 'proximity',
                                      dropunused = FALSE)
# collapse occasions, retain count detector type
cats_capts_sight_reduced <- reduce( cats_capts_sight, by = 'all')

# collapse occasions starting with proximity detector type and saving binomial counts
cats_capts_sight_reduced_prox <- reduce( cats_capts_sight_proximity, by = 'all', output = 'count')

# assemble list of capthist objects
chlist <- list(
    sight = cats_capts_sight,
    prox  = cats_capts_sight_proximity,
    red   = cats_capts_sight_reduced,
    redprox = cats_capts_sight_reduced_prox
)
sapply(chlist, summary, terse = T)
#            sight prox red redprox
# Occasions     46   46   1       1
# Detections   281  249 281     249
# Animals       94   94  94      94
# Detectors     88   88  88      88

# model fitting
# setting hessian = fdHess gives more reliable variances
# using default Newton-Raphson maximisation
baseargs <- list (
    mask = mask250, fixed = list(pID = 1), trace = FALSE,
    details = list(knownmarks = FALSE, distribution = 'binomial', hessian = 'fdHess'))

# binomN: counts treated as Poisson, but binomial when collapsing 46 binary occasions
fits <- list.secr.fit(constant = baseargs, capthist = chlist, binomN = c(0,0,0,1),
                      names = names(chlist))
sapply(fits, '[[', 'proctime')
# sight.elapsed    prox.elapsed     red.elapsed redprox.elapsed
# 102.64           12.98            4.70            1.49

predict(fits)
# $sight
# link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
# D       log   0.04512328 1.327761e-03   0.04259506   0.04780155
# g0    logit   0.01762068 4.053835e-05   0.01754140   0.01770031
# sigma   log 539.63674022 1.755961e+00 536.20608052 543.08934937
#
# $prox
# link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
# D       log   0.04688258  0.002458336   0.04230663   0.05195346
# g0    logit   0.01574333  0.001698774   0.01273806   0.01944367
# sigma   log 540.05998926 24.216483149 494.64427464 589.64554317
#
# $red
# link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
# D       log 1.165891e-01 1.473773e-06 1.165863e-01 1.165920e-01
# g0    logit 7.202355e-04 3.817195e-08 7.201607e-04 7.203103e-04
# sigma   log 8.291811e+02 3.804190e-02 8.291066e+02 8.292557e+02
#
# $redprox
# link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
# D       log   0.04803126  0.002544968   0.04329663   0.05328364
# g0    logit   0.01573369  0.001699207   0.01272792   0.01943532
# sigma   log 540.25305367 24.248391556 494.77942871 589.90601684

On Monday, September 16, 2024 at 9:10:39 AM UTC+9:30 murray...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi

I was able to tease out some of the issues with the (very tidy) data sent offline.

Mark-resight is tricky, frustrating, and prone to difficulties with model fitting, as you found.

Your use case is common enough and should be covered better in the documentation. An unknown fraction of the population carry natural marks.

The reason your model fits so quickly when you treat these as capture-recapture data (markocc all 1) rather than sighting-only mark-resight (markocc all zero) is that 'secr.fit' by default then collapses all occasions. This 'fastproximity' option is never invoked for sighting data, but you can emulate it manually as we will see.

Your initial data were of detector type 'count' (strictly 'count proximity' - potentially more than one detection per individual per camera per occasion). Binary proximity data (detector type 'proximity') are much faster to model. I also prefer proximity data in this case because they reduce potential pseudo-replication from repeat photographs at the same camera.

As I understand it, the data do not include a sighting category 'seen to be marked but not identified' (Tm NULL). Then we fix the parameter pID to avoid estimating it. Also for unknown marks we set the details argument knownmarks = FALSE.

Collapsing occasions is fairly simple - just use the reduce method for capthist objects with by = 'all' and a suitable outputdetector.
A coarser mask is justifiable - especially for exploration. For this dataset the spatial extent is set by the coastline and details distribution = 'binomial' is probably appropriate.

Here is a demonstration. Do not believe model fits with very small SE (e.g. fits[[3]] and perhaps sigma-hat from fits[[1]]). Remember these data are quirky, with many repeats at the same camera and a few camera-addicted individuals.

Murray

# mask250 is a 250-m mask
# cats_capts_sight is the full initial capthist dataset (46 occasions, includes sightings of unmarked Tu).

change detector type to 'proximity'
# dropunused set FALSE to avoid dropping occasion with zero detections
cats_capts_sight_proximity <- reduce( cats_capts_sight, output = 'proximity',
                                      dropunused = FALSE)
# collapse occasions, retain count detector type
cats_capts_sight_reduced <- reduce( cats_capts_sight, by = 'all')

# collapse occasions starting with proximity detector type and saving binomial counts
cats_capts_sight_reduced_prox <- reduce( cats_capts_sight_proximity, by = 'all', output = 'count')

# assemble list of capthist objects
chlist <- list(
    sight = cats_capts_sight,
    prox  = cats_capts_sight_proximity,
    red   = cats_capts_sight_reduced,
    redprox = cats_capts_sight_reduced_prox
)
sapply(chlist, summary, terse = T)
#            sight prox red redprox
# Occasions     46   46   1       1
# Detections   281  249 281     249
# Animals       94   94  94      94
# Detectors     88   88  88      88

# model fitting
# setting hessian = fdHess gives more reliable variances
# using default Newton-Raphson maximisation
baseargs <- list (
    mask = mask250, fixed = list(pID = 1), trace = FALSE,
    details = list(knownmarks = FALSE, distribution = 'binomial', hessian = 'fdHess'))

# binomN: counts treated as Poisson, but binomial when collapsing 46 binary occasions
fits <- list.secr.fit(constant = baseargs, capthist = chlist, binomN = c(0,0,0,1),
                      names = names(chlist))
sapply(fits, '[[', 'proctime')
# sight.elapsed    prox.elapsed     red.elapsed redprox.elapsed
# 102.64           12.98            4.70            1.49
